analysis|06-17|2018|Υπογράφεται η Συμφωνία των Πρεσπών|The Prespa Agreement is signed|After the breakup of Yugoslavia the neighbouring country declared independence in 1991 under the name "Macedonia", and Greece objected, considering that the name implied claims on its own region of the same name. For decades there were tensions and negotiations under the UN, and the issue blocked the neighbour's accession to NATO and the EU. // On 17 June 2018 the foreign ministers Nikos Kotzias and Nikola Dimitrov signed the agreement at Prespa, in the presence of prime ministers Alexis Tsipras and Zoran Zaev. It provided for the name "North Macedonia" for all uses. The agreement provoked strong reactions in Greece, with demonstrations and political confrontation. // The agreement was ratified by the two parliaments in early 2019. North Macedonia joined NATO in 2020 and moved towards European integration, while the agreement remains a subject of political dispute and is sometimes interpreted differently by the two sides.

analysis|06-18|1953|Οι Έλληνες στρατιώτες αποκρούουν την επίθεση στο ύψωμα Χάρρυ|Greek soldiers repel the attack on Harry Hill|When the Korean War broke out in 1950, Greece sent an expeditionary force within the framework of the UN forces. It was a country that had just emerged from the civil war, and participation was a way to show alignment with the West, but also to strengthen ties with the United States. // In summer 1953, shortly before the armistice, the Chinese launched fierce attacks on forward positions, among them the hill the Americans called "Harry". Greek forces took part in the defence of the area and faced hard hand-to-hand battles. // The armistice was signed on 27 July 1953. The participation of the Greek contingent, which had killed and wounded, was regarded as important for Greece's prestige as an ally. The Greek army honours the memory of the fallen, and Korea remains an example of Greek presence in international missions.

analysis|06-18|1989|Διπλές εκλογές χωρίς αυτοδυναμία|Elections without an outright majority|In 1989 the political life of Greece had been affected by scandals, chiefly that of Koskotas and the Bank of Crete, which struck the PASOK government and Andreas Papandreou. The elections of 18 June coincided with the European elections, and were held under proportional representation, a system that made it difficult to form a single-party government. // New Democracy of Konstantinos Mitsotakis came first but had no majority of seats, and PASOK could not cooperate with it. There followed a coalition government of New Democracy with the Coalition of the Left under Tzannis Tzannetakis, with the aim of cleansing political life. // After new elections in November a grand coalition was formed under Xenophon Zolotas, which dealt with investigating the scandals and with political stabilisation. In 1990 new elections gave New Democracy a narrow majority and Mitsotakis the premiership.

analysis|06-19|1913|Αρχίζει η μάχη Κιλκίς–Λαχανά|The battle of Kilkis–Lachanas begins|After the Bulgarian attack during the night towards 17 June by the old calendar, the Greek army, led by King Constantine, went over to the counter-offensive. The Bulgarians held fortified positions north of Thessaloniki, in the area of Kilkis and Lachanas, and wanted to keep control of Macedonia. // The battle, which lasted about three days, was hard, with heavy losses on both sides. The Greeks took the Bulgarian positions and forced the enemy to withdraw northward. It was the most important battle of the Second Balkan War for Greece. // The victory consolidated Greek control of Thessaloniki and Macedonia and strengthened the prestige of the Greek army and of King Constantine. The army then advanced further north, and the war ended within a few weeks with the Treaty of Bucharest, which confirmed the Greek conquests.

analysis|06-19|1958|Το σχέδιο Μακμίλαν για την Κύπρο|The Macmillan plan for Cyprus|Since 1955 Cyprus had lived through the armed struggle of EOKA against British rule, with the demand for union with Greece. The Turkish Cypriots and Turkey opposed this and demanded partition, and the clash between the communities had already begun. Britain was looking for a solution that would preserve its interests on the island. // Prime Minister Harold Macmillan presented his plan in June 1958. It provided for a seven-year transitional regime with the participation of Greece and Turkey in the administration, and for separate communal councils. The Greek Cypriot leadership, headed by Makarios, rejected it, because it saw in it the consolidation of division. // The rejection was accompanied by increased violence on the island. The negotiations continued and in 1959 ended in the Zurich and London agreements, which led to Cypriot independence in 1960, without union and without partition.

analysis|06-19|1975|Ο Κωνσταντίνος Τσάτσος εκλέγεται Πρόεδρος της Δημοκρατίας|Konstantinos Tsatsos is elected President of the Republic|After the fall of the dictatorship in 1974 and the referendum of December that decided in favour of a republic without a king, the country had a provisional president. The new Constitution was voted by Parliament in June 1975 and provided for a President of the Republic elected by Parliament. // Parliament elected Konstantinos Tsatsos, lawyer, philosopher and politician, a collaborator of Konstantinos Karamanlis, with 210 votes. He was the first president under the new Constitution, and his election showed the broad consensus that existed in the political system at the time. // Tsatsos remained in office until 1980, when he was succeeded by Karamanlis. His presidency coincided with the consolidation of democracy and the negotiations for accession to the EEC. The Constitution of 1975 defined the country's political system for decades, with amendments in 1986, 2001, 2008 and 2019.

analysis|06-20|1975|Ο Τσάτσος πρόεδρος της Δημοκρατίας|Tsatsos as President of the Republic|Konstantinos Tsatsos was born in 1899 and was professor of the philosophy of law, with a rich body of writings. He had served as minister in Karamanlis's governments, especially in the field of Culture, and was known for his broad learning. His election to the highest office of the state came in a period of transition. // After the dictatorship the country needed a figure of common acceptance in the presidency, and Tsatsos was regarded as suitable to embody the continuity of the state. His election by Parliament in June 1975 was carried by a very large majority. // His term covered the first years of the Metapolitefsi. He remained in office until 1980. His presidency is regarded as a period of institutional stabilisation, after the dramatic events of the junta and Cyprus, and it helped establish the notion that the President is an institution above the parties.

analysis|06-20|1978|Ο σεισμός της Θεσσαλονίκης|The Thessaloniki earthquake|Thessaloniki and the wider area lie in a seismic zone, and there was always the danger of a major earthquake. The constructions of the period were not always resistant, which is why seismic danger was a frequent subject of discussion. The earthquake struck while the city was in motion, so that several citizens were injured in the streets. // On 20 June 1978 a tremor of magnitude 6.5 on the Richter scale, with its epicentre in the area of Volvi, shook the city, and aftershocks followed that worried residents. The intensity of the earthquake was great in the surrounding areas too. Emergency services were mobilised immediately for rescue and assistance. // The earthquake caused 50 deaths and major damage to buildings in the city and in the surrounding villages, while villages in the Volvi area were also hit. The damage took time to repair. The event brought back the question of anti-seismic protection and control of construction. Thessaloniki was rebuilt and recovered, but the experience became a lesson on the need for prevention and anti-seismic regulations. The experience of the earthquake contributed to shaping modern anti-seismic rules. The scale of the damage to buildings contributed to the discussion about the modern anti-seismic engineering of the city.

analysis|06-21|2019|Πεθαίνει ο Δημήτρης Χριστόφιας|Dimitris Christofias dies|Dimitris Christofias was born in 1946 and rose through the ranks of AKEL, the Progressive Party of the Working People, the party of the Left in Cyprus. From 1988 to 2009 he was general secretary of the party and was regarded as a strong personality in the political life of the island. // In 2008 he was elected President of the Republic of Cyprus. During his term he held talks with the Turkish Cypriot leader on the Cyprus problem, and Cyprus took over the EU presidency in 2012. // His term was marked by the explosion at the naval base "Evangelos Florakis" in 2011, with thirteen dead, and by the economic crisis that broke out towards the end of his term. He died in 2019, at the age of 72.

analysis|06-22|431|Αρχίζει η Γ΄ Οικουμενική Σύνοδος|The Third Ecumenical Council begins|In the early 5th century Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, taught that Mary should be called Christotokos and not Theotokos, because the divine and human natures of Christ were separate. This view provoked the reaction of Cyril of Alexandria and divided the Church. Emperor Theodosius II convened a synod at Ephesus. // The synod began in June 431, and Nestorius, who disagreed with the way it was organised, did not take part in the first sessions. The bishops of the synod condemned his teaching and deposed him, and confirmed the title "Theotokos" for the Virgin Mary. // The decisions led to a division: the followers of Nestorius withdrew, and later the Church of the East was formed, which spread to Persia and as far as Central Asia. The synod shaped basic elements of Christology and of the veneration of the Virgin in Orthodox tradition and in other Christian traditions.

analysis|06-23|1897|Γεννιέται ο Γεώργιος Γρίβας|Georgios Grivas is born|Georgios Grivas was born in 1897 in Trikomo, in Famagusta, when Cyprus was administered by Britain, although its sovereignty was still nominally Ottoman. He later settled in Greece, where he followed a military career and acquired Greek citizenship. // He served in the Greek army and during the Occupation founded the organisation "X". In the 1950s, with the encouragement of Archbishop Makarios, he organised the EOKA struggle for the liberation of Cyprus from British administration and its union with Greece. The struggle began on 1 April 1955, and under the pseudonym "Digenis" Grivas directed the guerrilla war. // The struggle ended in 1959 with the Zurich and London agreements, which created an independent Republic of Cyprus without union. Later Grivas returned to Cyprus and opposed Makarios, founding EOKA B. He died in 1974. Assessments of his role differ: for many he was a hero of the struggle, while others judge him for his choices after 1960.

analysis|06-23|1996|Πεθαίνει ο Ανδρέας Παπανδρέου|Andreas Papandreou dies|Andreas Papandreou was born in 1919, was the son of Georgios Papandreou, and studied economics in the United States, where he pursued an academic career. He returned to Greece and engaged in politics, but was arrested by the junta in 1967 and later left for abroad, where he carried out anti-dictatorship activity. // After the Metapolitefsi he founded PASOK in 1974 and led it from a small party to the winner of the elections of 1981, when he became prime minister. He was prime minister until 1989 and again from 1993 to 1996. His government established reforms in social policy, such as the National Health System and the recognition of the National Resistance, but also policies that were debated intensely. // He resigned in January 1996 for health reasons and died in Athens on 23 June. His funeral gathered large crowds, and his rise changed the political map of the country. Kostas Simitis succeeded him as prime minister, and his son Giorgos Papandreou later also became prime minister.

analysis|06-24|1798|Θανατώνεται ο Ρήγας Βελεστινλής|Rigas Velestinlis is executed|Rigas Velestinlis was born in Velestino in Thessaly and lived in Vienna, influenced by the ideas of the Enlightenment and the French Revolution. He envisioned a multinational democracy in the Balkans, in place of the Ottoman Empire, where all peoples, regardless of religion, would have equal rights. He wrote the "New Political Administration" and the "Thourios" about this. // In 1797 he tried to travel to the Balkans to organise the movement, but was arrested in Trieste by the Austrian authorities. The Austrians handed him over to the Ottomans, and he was transferred to Belgrade. There he was executed with companions in June 1798, and according to tradition his body was thrown into the Danube. // Rigas did not see his plans realised, but his work and death became a symbol. The ideals of freedom and equality that he spread influenced Greeks and other Balkan peoples, and he is regarded as a forerunner of the Philiki Etaireia and of the Revolution of 1821.

analysis|06-25|1925|Ο Πάγκαλος καταλύει τη Δημοκρατία|Pangalos overthrows the Republic|The Second Hellenic Republic, founded in 1924 after the abolition of the monarchy, was weak and unstable. The Asia Minor Catastrophe, the political division between royalists and Venizelists, and continuous military interventions had created a political crisis. General Theodoros Pangalos was known for his participation in the revolution of 1922. // In June 1925 Pangalos overthrew the government with a military movement and declared a dictatorship. He dissolved Parliament, restricted freedoms and governed by decree. In 1926 he became President of the Republic after elections that were regarded as a sham. // The dictatorship ended in August 1926, when General Georgios Kondylis overthrew him. The period was a warning about the large involvement of the army in political life, a phenomenon that continued throughout the interwar period and peaked in the movement of 1935 and the dictatorship of Metaxas in 1936.

analysis|06-25|2023|Δεύτερες εθνικές εκλογές του έτους|Second national elections of the year|The elections of 21 May 2023 were held under a system of simple proportional representation, and New Democracy of Kyriakos Mitsotakis came first by a wide margin, but had no majority. Under the Constitution and the law, no government was formed and a second ballot was called. A caretaker government managed the transitional period. // On 25 June the vote took place under a system that gave a bonus of seats to the first party. New Democracy increased its share and won an outright majority. SYRIZA, which came second, suffered a heavy defeat. Alexis Tsipras resigned the party leadership shortly afterwards. // Kyriakos Mitsotakis continued as prime minister for a second four-year term. The elections showed the strong position of New Democracy in the political scene, while the opposition was fragmented. It was also the first time since 2015 that the country had two parliamentary elections in the same year.

analysis|06-26|2007|Ο καύσωνας των 47,5°C|The heatwave of 47.5°C|The summer of 2007 was one of the hottest Greece had experienced, with a prolonged heatwave that affected south-eastern Europe. In late June temperatures rose to very high levels, and according to the records reached 47.5 degrees Celsius in areas of Greece, a record for the last decades. // The heat caused problems with electricity supply, since the demand for air conditioning was very high, and there were many cases of heatstroke, especially among the elderly. With dry forests and strong winds, large fires broke out, with a major one on Parnitha. // The summer of 2007 became historic also because of the destructive fires of August in the Peloponnese and in Evia. The heatwave brought to public debate the question of forest protection, the prevention of fires and adaptation to climate change, issues that remain topical.

analysis|06-27|1929|Ιδρύεται η Αγροτική Τράπεζα της Ελλάδος|The Agricultural Bank of Greece is founded|At the end of the 1920s Greek agriculture needed organised credit. Farmers often borrowed from private individuals at high interest, and the large refugee settlement in the countryside had increased the needs. The government of Eleftherios Venizelos placed great weight on the modernisation of agriculture and the strengthening of production. // In 1929 the Agricultural Bank of Greece was founded, which took on the financing of agricultural production, with low-interest loans and support for cooperatives. // For more than eight decades the ATE was a basic lever of the agricultural economy. In the years of the economic crisis, however, it faced serious problems and in 2012 its assets passed to Piraeus Bank. Its history shows the role of the state in supporting the countryside and the limits of that policy.

analysis|06-27|1976|Η αεροπειρατεία της πτήσης 139 της Air France|The hijacking of Air France flight 139|On 27 June 1976 an aircraft of Air France operating the route Tel Aviv–Athens–Paris set off from Athens with passengers from many countries. After take-off it was seized by a group that included Palestinians and Germans, who demanded the release of prisoners. // The aircraft was eventually taken to Entebbe airport in Uganda, where the hijackers held the hostages. The hijackers released some passengers but kept the Israelis and other Jews, which provoked international reaction. After negotiations, Israel organised a rescue operation. // The Entebbe operation, carried out on the night of 3 to 4 July, freed most of the hostages, but there were deaths. The event revealed gaps in airport security, and the fact that the hijackers had boarded in Athens led to discussion about the security measures of the Greek airport.

analysis|06-27|2015|Ανακοινώνεται δημοψήφισμα|A referendum is announced|After the election of the SYRIZA-ANEL government in January 2015, negotiations with the lenders on extending the support programme dragged on for months without agreement. The programme was due to expire at the end of June, and Greece had large obligations to the IMF. The lenders proposed measures and reforms that the government considered unacceptable. // On the evening of Saturday 27 June Alexis Tsipras announced in a televised address that a referendum would be held on the lenders' proposal, and asked citizens to reject it. In the Eurogroup the partners reacted negatively, and the European Central Bank did not raise the limit of emergency liquidity. // The next day capital controls were imposed and the banks were closed. The referendum took place on 5 July and the "No" won, but a few days later the government agreed to a new programme with harsher terms, and the period remained in collective memory as one of the most intense of the crisis.

analysis|06-28|1979|Η Βουλή κυρώνει τη συνθήκη προσχώρησης στην ΕΟΚ|Parliament ratifies the EEC accession treaty|Greece had applied for membership of the European Economic Community in 1975, a year after the Metapolitefsi. The government of Konstantinos Karamanlis saw accession as a guarantee for democracy and as a support for the economy. The accession treaty had been signed in Athens on 28 May 1979. // On 28 June Parliament ratified it, in spite of objections from opposition parties, which feared the consequences for the Greek economy and national independence. The government majority carried the ratification. // Greece became a full member on 1 January 1981, as the tenth member of the Community. Accession brought funds, new markets and institutional links with the West, but also adjustments for agriculture and industry. PASOK, when it governed from 1981, asked for a change of terms, but the country remained in the Community.

analysis|06-28|2015|Η Ελλάδα ξυπνά με κλειστές τράπεζες|Greece wakes up to closed banks|After the announcement of the referendum on Saturday 27 June 2015, Greeks rushed to withdraw money from the ATMs, and the queues multiplied. The European Central Bank did not increase the emergency liquidity for the Greek banks, and there was a risk that their cash would run out. // On 28 June the government announced the banking holiday and the imposition of capital controls. The banks remained closed from Monday 29 June, and withdrawals were limited to 60 euros a day per card. Transactions with abroad were subject to restrictions. // The banks reopened around 20 July, after the referendum and the agreement with the lenders, but capital controls remained in force for years, until September 2019. The events affected the economy, businesses and the daily life of citizens, and were one of the most important episodes of the Greek crisis.

analysis|06-29|1850|Αυτοκέφαλη η Εκκλησία της Ελλάδος|The Church of Greece becomes autocephalous|After the Revolution of 1821 the Church in the liberated areas operated without connection to the Patriarchate of Constantinople, which was under Ottoman rule. The regency of Otto, on the proposal of Georgios Maurer and Theoklitos Farmakidis, declared the Church of Greece autocephalous in 1833, without seeking the consent of the Patriarch. // The Patriarchate did not at first recognise the action, and there was a rupture. After years of negotiations, the Patriarchal Tomos of 1850 was issued, which officially recognised the autocephaly of the Church of Greece and its independence from the Patriarchate in administration. // The settlement resolved a major dispute and gave a legal basis to the administration of the Church in the Greek state. However, the relations of the Patriarchate with the Church of Greece and the jurisdictional areas, such as the "New Lands", remained a matter of discussion and settlement in the 20th century.

analysis|06-30|1913|Η σφαγή του Δοξάτου|The Doxato massacre|In the Second Balkan War Bulgaria fought Greece and Serbia for control of Macedonia. When the Bulgarian forces were forced to withdraw, the war turned into a harsh field of reprisals against the populations. In the area of Drama there were Greek and Bulgarian villages, and the region was the scene of critical operations. // At Doxato, a town of eastern Macedonia, Bulgarian troops and irregulars gathered the inhabitants, killed hundreds of Greeks and set fire to the houses. The destruction of Doxato became known internationally and was recorded in the report of the Carnegie Commission, which investigated the atrocities of the Balkan Wars. // Doxato was rebuilt, and the memory of the massacre is kept with a monument and events. The area of Drama passed definitively to Greece with the Treaty of Bucharest. The event recalls the violence that accompanied the Balkan Wars and the role of civilians as victims, a phenomenon repeated in the 20th century.

analysis|07-01|1097|Η μάχη του Δορυλαίου|The battle of Dorylaeum|The First Crusade began after the appeal of Pope Urban II in 1095, partly in response to a request for help from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who was facing the Seljuk Turks in Asia Minor. The crusaders, mainly Frankish knights, passed through Constantinople and moved through Anatolia, having already taken Nicaea with Byzantine cooperation. // Near Dorylaeum, in Phrygia, the army of the Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan attacked the advanced detachment of the crusaders, led by Bohemond of Taranto. The crusaders held on until the rest of the army arrived, and the Turks finally withdrew with considerable losses. // The victory opened the way to southern Asia Minor and Syria and helped Byzantium recover part of the western coasts of Asia Minor. The crusaders reached Jerusalem in 1099. The clash showed both the strength of the Frankish heavy cavalry and the difficulties their cooperation with Byzantium would have in the following years.

analysis|07-01|1570|Οι Οθωμανοί αποβιβάζονται στην Κύπρο|The Ottomans land in Cyprus|Since 1489 Cyprus had been a Venetian possession, which used it as a trading base in the Eastern Mediterranean. Sultan Selim II wanted to conquer it, since the island was close to the Ottoman coasts and important for control of the sea routes. Venice sought help from other European powers, but did not receive it in time. // In summer 1570 the Ottoman fleet and army, led by Lala Mustafa Pasha, landed on Cyprus near Larnaca. The siege of Nicosia followed, which fell in September 1570 with great massacres. Famagusta resisted much longer and surrendered in August 1571. // The Ottoman conquest brought changes in administration, in social structure and in the composition of the population, with the settlement of Muslims on the island and changes in the position of the Orthodox Church. Cyprus remained Ottoman until 1878, when it passed to British administration. The naval battle of Lepanto, in October 1571, came too late to save the island.

analysis|07-01|1828|Αρχίζει η λειτουργία της Σχολής Ευελπίδων|The Evelpidon Military Academy begins operating|After Ioannis Kapodistrias arrived in Greece in 1828, the new state needed an organised army and trained officers. During the Revolution the military forces often consisted of irregular bodies, and Kapodistrias wanted to create a regular army and military training. // The "Evelpidon Lochos" was founded at Nafplio, a body of young men who would be trained as officers. The candidates were young men who wished to serve as officers. Training included military and general subjects. // The school was later moved to Athens and took the name Evelpidon Military Academy. It is the oldest military academy in Greece, and many officers of the Greek army, among them leading figures of the country's history, studied there. Its foundation shows Kapodistrias's effort to organise institutions in the newly formed state.

analysis|07-01|2004|Η Ελλάδα προκρίνεται στον τελικό του Euro 2004|Greece reaches the final of Euro 2004|Greece went to Euro 2004 in Portugal as a team that was not considered favourite, coached by the German Otto Rehhagel. In the group stage it beat Portugal in the opening match, drew with Spain and went through to the quarter-finals. There it beat the holders France 1-0. // In the semi-final it faced the Czech Republic, which was regarded as one of the best teams of the tournament. The match was goalless in normal time, and in extra time, at the end of the first half of the extra period, Traianos Dellas scored with a header from a corner. Under the "golden goal" rule then in force, the match ended immediately after the first half of extra time. // The victory took Greece to the final and led to one of the most impressive results in European football. The team relied on a solid defence and collective spirit. The success gave rise to enthusiasm throughout the country and showed that organisation can beat teams with more stars.

analysis|07-01|2012|Η Κύπρος αναλαμβάνει την προεδρία του Συμβουλίου της ΕΕ|Cyprus takes over the Presidency of the EU Council|Cyprus became a member of the European Union in 2004, and the Presidency of the Council rotates every six months among the member states. Cyprus's turn was foreseen for the second half of 2012, and the country prepared to organise meetings and to manage the agenda of the Union. // From 1 July 2012 Cyprus took over the Presidency for the first time. The period coincided with the economic crisis in the eurozone and with negotiations on the EU's multi-annual budget. As presiding state the country had to act as a mediator and not to promote its own interests. // It was a test for a small state, which also coincided with internal economic problems: in 2013 Cyprus needed a support programme. The Presidency nevertheless remained important for the country's image and for its place in the European family. Cyprus took over the Presidency again in 2026.

analysis|07-02|1974|Ο Μακάριος γράφει στον Ιωαννίδη|Makarios writes to Ioannides|In the early 1970s the relations of Makarios with the Greek military government in Athens had deteriorated. Makarios was President of Cyprus and wanted an independent policy, while the National Guard was commanded by Greek officers and EOKA B, which was supported from Athens, acted against him. In Athens Brigadier Dimitrios Ioannides was powerful. // On 2 July 1974 Makarios sent a letter to the President of Greece, Phaedon Gizikis, which he made public shortly afterwards. He accused the Greek officers of the National Guard of conspiring against him and asked for the removal of the Greek officers. // The letter sharpened the crisis. On 15 July 1974 the officers of the National Guard, with the support of the junta, carried out a coup, and Makarios fled. Turkey invaded Cyprus on 20 July. The events led to the division of the island, to the fall of the dictatorship in Greece and to a problem that remains unresolved.

analysis|07-03|1908|Ανακαλύπτεται ο Δίσκος της Φαιστού|The Phaistos Disc is discovered|The palace of Phaistos, in southern Crete, was one of the great centres of Minoan civilisation. An Italian archaeological mission had carried out excavations there from the early 20th century, and Luigi Pernier continued the work after the first excavators. // On 3 July 1908 Pernier found a round clay disc in a small room of the palace. On both sides there are spiral symbols, which were impressed with seals before the clay was fired. It is dated to the 2nd millennium BC. // The disc is a unique find, since its symbols have not been found elsewhere, and its script has not been deciphered despite many attempts. Many explanations have been proposed, but none has become generally accepted. It is displayed in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum and remains one of the greatest enigmas of archaeology.

analysis|07-04|1822|Η μάχη του Πέτα|The battle of Peta|In 1822 the Ottomans were preparing to regain Epirus and Roumeli, and the government of Alexandros Mavrokordatos wanted to help the Souliotes, who were under siege. For this purpose an expeditionary force was sent to Epirus, with the Philhellenic Battalion, under the German Karl von Norman, and Greek fighters. // At Peta in Arta the Greeks and the philhellenes clashed with the Ottoman army, which was numerous and well organised. The conditions for the Greek side were difficult, and the battle ended in a heavy defeat. The Philhellenic Battalion suffered great losses. // The defeat led the Souliotes to come to terms with the Ottomans and to abandon Souli, and the Ottomans advanced towards Roumeli. Despite the defeat, the Revolution continued, and Missolonghi resisted the siege in the autumn. Mavrokordatos became a target of criticism, but kept an important role in what followed.

analysis|07-04|1990|Η Κύπρος υποβάλλει αίτηση ένταξης στην ΕΟΚ|Cyprus applies for membership of the EEC|Cyprus had had an association agreement with the European Economic Community since 1972, and in the 1980s developed its economy. After the Turkish invasion of 1974 the island was divided, but the government of the Republic of Cyprus wanted to strengthen its international position through European accession. // On 4 July 1990 the government of President George Vassiliou formally submitted an application for membership of the Community. The process took years: negotiations for accession began in 1998, together with other candidate countries. // Cyprus became a member of the European Union on 1 May 2004, even though the government's control did not extend to the occupied areas. The result came after the rejection of the Annan Plan by Greek Cypriots. Accession brought new opportunities and obligations, and Cyprus joined the euro area in 2008.

analysis|07-04|2004|Η Ελλάδα πρωταθλήτρια Ευρώπης στο ποδόσφαιρο|Greece is European football champion|The Greek national team had taken part in very few major tournaments before 2004, and had never passed the group stage. The German coach Otto Rehhagel had built a team with a strong defence and team discipline, with players such as Angelos Charisteas, Theodoros Zagorakis and Traianos Dellas. // In the final in Lisbon Greece faced Portugal, the host of the tournament, which was the favourite and which Greece had beaten in the opening match. Charisteas scored with a header in the 57th minute, and Greece held the 1-0 lead to the end, with disciplined defence. // Greece became European champion, which was regarded as a great surprise. The success brought great celebrations and enthusiasm to the country, a few months before the Olympic Games in Athens. The victory remains the greatest in the history of Greek football.

analysis|07-05|2015|Το δημοψήφισμα του 2015|The 2015 referendum|After the election of the SYRIZA-ANEL government in January 2015, negotiations with the lenders to complete the support programme did not reach agreement. At the end of June Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras announced a referendum on the lenders' proposal, and the banks closed, with restrictions on withdrawals. // The referendum took place on 5 July, in an atmosphere of intense polarisation. The question was whether to accept the agreement draft submitted by the institutions, and the "No" prevailed with about 61% of the votes.
